title: The first nativity scene
hook: at Greccio, Francis sets up a manger with a real ox and donkey

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis and the Sultan al-Kamil, and your line was crossing the lines. Who got a real courtesy from you, and how did it land? Day eight hundred sixteen.

Christmas night, in a small hill town called Greccio, in Italy. Men and women from the area are climbing toward a spot near the woods, carrying candles and torches that light up the dark. Friars have come in from other places. Waiting for them is a manger, filled with hay. Beside it stand an ox and a donkey. Real ones, breathing in the cold. And next to the manger stands Francis of Assisi, singing the Gospel in a clear voice. Today's word is that scene, and the reason he set it up.

Thomas of Celano, Francis's early biographer, tells why. Francis asked a man of Greccio named John to help him prepare it, because, in paraphrase, he wanted to see with his own bodily eyes the hardship the baby went through: how he was laid in a manger, how he lay on hay with an ox and a donkey standing by. Not a painting. Not an idea. A real manger. Look at the Gospel's own words. Luke, in the King James Version: "she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." A manger is a feeding trough. And notice: Luke never mentions an ox or a donkey. They come from a line in Isaiah that Christian tradition set beside the birth story: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." At Greccio the two texts stood side by side, in hay and breath. Then, Celano says, Mass was celebrated over the manger, and Francis preached about the child of Bethlehem, saying the name with great tenderness. A man there, Celano adds, saw in a vision a child lying still in the manger, and Francis bending to wake him. Celano reads that as a picture of the whole night: a child who'd been forgotten in many hearts, woken up again. Tradition calls Greccio the first nativity scene. Whatever came before it, the custom it's remembered for lives on, in cribs set out in churches and homes, some grand, some small enough to sit on a windowsill.
screen: `THE OX AND DONKEY COME FROM ISAIAH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one small, real thing. If you have a nativity set, take out one piece and set it where you'll see it today. If not, any small object will do: a cup, a stone, a folded cloth, set down on purpose as a place for something to arrive. Then sit with it, and breathe. If you pray, you can let it be a manger, an empty place made ready. If you don't, let it stand for something you want to make real, not just think about. The bell holds the time.
Nativity scene. What tradition calls the first one, at Greccio, where Francis set out a real manger, with hay, an ox and a donkey, so people could see the story with their own eyes.
Your line: a real manger. Today, take one hope you usually keep as an idea and give it one physical form: set it out, write it down, or do it with your hands. Day eight hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Churches and Christian homes often set out a nativity scene, or crib, during Advent and Christmas; some places hold living nativities with people and animals, and some families add the figure of the baby only on Christmas Eve.

original.note: Greek: a manger, a feeding trough — the word in Luke 2:7.

trapdoor: what you thought: a decoration that comes out with the tree.
what it means: Francis's way of seeing the poverty of Jesus's birth with his own eyes: a real manger, real hay, real animals.
what a scholar hears: Thomas of Celano's account of Greccio, and an ox and donkey that come from Isaiah, not from Luke.

notes: The year 1223 (in the index hook) is not spoken under the claims rule; the hook field drops it. Confirm.
The title's 'first' is the index's; the spoken text says 'as tradition calls it' and 'whatever came before it'. Confirm the framing.

Celano, First Life 84–86: Francis asks John of Greccio to prepare, wanting to see with bodily eyes the infant's hardships; people come with candles and torches; brothers summoned from many places; manger, hay, ox and ass; Mass over the manger; Francis as deacon sings the Gospel and preaches, saying 'the babe of Bethlehem' tenderly; a man's vision of a lifeless child roused by Francis, read by Celano as the child forgotten in many hearts being awakened. Paraphrased; confirm.

'Christians have long read [Isaiah 1:3] beside the birth story': the ox and ass tradition also draws on the apocryphal Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew and Habakkuk 3:2 (Old Latin/LXX). Confirm the simplification.
howItsDone says churches and homes often set out a crib; confirm.
Original: φάτνη in Luke 2:7; confirm the pronunciation.

Editor pass: cut the repeated "detail to repeat tonight" formula (also used on day 809 and 799) and softened the Isaiah 1:3 line to "Christian tradition set beside" rather than a claim about what Christians read.

Second editor pass: Celano does not say Francis was thinking of Isaiah, so 'Francis put the two texts side by side' became 'at Greccio the two texts stood side by side'; changed the practice's first 'If you don't' (no nativity set) to 'If not' so it doesn't blur with the later 'If you don't' (pray).
Audit: replaced a strawman myth (imagining the scene 'with eyes closed', which nobody claims) with the vision Celano reports, which the teach covers.
